name: Shape L - Pronunciation Noticing (Noticing-First)
description: Noticing-first pronunciation lesson for a specific L1-transfer feature (e.g. dropped/underarticulated word-final /t/, /d/, /Id/ endings for Thai learners). Learners are first made to HEAR the gap between the L1-transfer version and the target (auditory discrimination), then the feature is isolated, linked to meaning, drilled, and used freely. Authentic recordings from past students serve as the final noticing text.
pedagogical_justification:
Pronunciation instruction that works is intelligibility-based (Levis, 2005; Munro & Derwing, 1995) and noticing-first (Schmidt, 1990): learners must consciously notice a feature in input for it to become intake, and instruction is most effective when it primes that noticing (Schmidt & Frota, 1986). For Thai learners, word-final /t/ and /d/ are the critical case: Thai final stops are unreleased but phonologically present, so learners believe they are pronouncing the consonant when listeners hear nothing. Final-consonant deletion and missing clusters are the strongest intelligibility threats in Thai-accented English (Setter, 2005; Suntornsawet, 2022). The shape therefore follows the perception-before-production sequence established in final-consonant-deletion intervention: auditory discrimination precedes production.

The shape embeds four design principles learned in practice:
(1) PERCEPTUAL SALIENCE IS DESIGNED, NOT ASSUMED. Model sentences place every target sound before a vowel or a pause, where native speakers audibly release the consonant. Coarticulation traps ("wanted to", "fight game", "last night") are unusable as models because natives reduce them too.
(2) THE GAP IS MADE AUDIBLE WITH A CONTRAST PAIR. The trigger stage plays a comparison track: a narrator labels "Thai English" then "Standard English" readings of the same model sentence (native model + homophone-respelled version produced by TTS).
(3) TARGETS ARE NUMBERED, KEYS ARE AUDITED. Noticing texts carry numbered underlined targets ([0] = example item, [1]-[n] = scored targets). The tick/cross answer key CANNOT be inferred from the audio metadata - it must be verified by a teacher listening to the recording (LLM-as-judge and regex checks cannot hear dropped consonants).
(4) AUTHENTIC STUDENT DATA IS THE FINAL INPUT. The closing stage uses a real past-student recording (from assessment audio) as an authentic noticing text: the transcript is corrected ONLY in the target feature (all other grammar left verbatim), targets are underlined and numbered, and students tick/cross the recording against the printed text.

The trigger stage contrasts a model sentence against the L1-transfer version; the feature stage isolates the target (including the -ed /Id/ syllable, which Thai has no equivalent for) and links it to meaning (dropped -ed hides past tense); controlled production drills the release; freer use transfers it into spontaneous speech. In-class assessment data grounds the choice of feature: 112 students (27% of the cohort) carry examiner feedback flagging dropped or underarticulated final /t/, /d/, or -ed endings. Stage times assume a 46-minute lesson.
main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to notice and produce [target feature] in the context of [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to notice and produce word-final /t/, /d/ and /Id/ endings (including -ed) in the context of talking about what they did last night.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
[DD-MM-YY]
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
L (Pronunciation Noticing)
Materials:
Slideshow, worksheet (Parts A-H), comparison audio, Part B and Part C tracks, Rome recording, quantum model audio
Assessment:
Discrimination accuracy (Parts A-C), production observation during drills and the game (Part F)
Systems:
Pronunciation

stages.stage_aim: To activate the topic and elicit the target feature in natural speech
stages.procedure:
- Show the splash slide. Ask: What do you see? What might this lesson be about? Let students speculate.
- Advance to the title slide. Confirm the theme: the sounds at the end of words.
- Ask: What did you do last night? Elicit 3-4 answers. Write them on the board exactly as students say them, without comment.
- Tell students the focus is the sounds at the END of words.

stages.stage_aim: To make the gap between L1 transfer and the target audible
stages.procedure:
- Display the model sentence: I started my game at eight and played it all night. Every target sits before a vowel or a pause (salience-designed).
- Play the comparison track: a narrator labels Thai English, then Standard English, readings of the model sentence.
- Ask: Can you hear the difference? What disappeared?
- Students tap the table on every final /t/ or /d/ they hear in the Standard English version (Worksheet, Part A).
- Feedback: the model sentence has five final sounds: started, eight, played, it, night.

stages.stage_aim: To perceive the target feature before producing it
stages.procedure:
- Worksheet, Part B. Play the track: a narrator announces each number, a second voice says each word twice.
- Students write ✓ if both repetitions are correct, or ✗ if the final sound is dropped.
- Check answers against the audited key (verified by listening, never guessed). Pattern: ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓.
- Repeat any pairs students could not perceive. Note who still cannot hear the difference.

stages.stage_aim: To isolate the /t/, /d/, /Id/ endings and link them to meaning
stages.procedure:
- Worksheet, Part C. Play the track: each past-tense verb read once. Students write ✓ if they hear the -ed ending, or ✗ if it is missing.
- Check answers: wanted ✓, played ✗, stopped ✓, needed ✗, watched ✓, stayed ✓, started ✗, helped ✓.
- Worksheet, Part D. Students clap the syllables. Reveal one count per click: wanted = 3, played = 1, stopped = 1, needed = 2.
- Elicit the rule: after /t/ or /d/, -ed adds a syllable. Worksheet, Part E: circle the past tense - want is present, wanted is past.

- Finger-tap drill on the model sentence: I started (1) my game at eight (2) and played (3) it (4) all night (5).
- Backchain: night, all night, played it all night, I started my game at eight and played it all night.
- Choral and individual drill. Whisper-release drill: night, played - the final consonant must be heard.
- Correct errors immediately. -ed words keep their extra syllable.

stages.stage_aim: To transfer the feature into spontaneous speech
stages.procedure:
- Worksheet, Part F. Show the game slide and start the 5-minute timer.
- Pairs: A tells B two things they did last night. B holds up one finger for every final /t/ or /d/ heard - one point per sound.
- Dropped final = do-over until B hears it. Swap after 2.5 minutes.
- Content feedback first, then language feedback on the most frequent dropped finals.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate noticing on authentic student speech and set up recycling
stages.procedure:
- Worksheet, Part G. Play a past student's recording (from assessment audio). Students tick or cross the numbered underlined targets.
- The transcript is corrected ONLY in the target feature; all other grammar stays verbatim. [0] is the example item.
- Reveal the audited key (e.g. only [5], [10], [22] and [23] were correct).
- Worksheet, Part H. Play the model reading. Pairs read the paragraph to each other and tick or cross.
- Quick-fire exit: night, wanted, played. Say them with the ending. Tell students the finals return in the next warm-up.
